items.prose: A fixed-income desk trains a small tokeniser on its notes. It learns five merges, in this order: 256 is `o n`, 257 is 256 then `d`, 258 is `b` then 257, 259 is a space then 258, and 260 is `u n`. It now encodes `bonds fund bond`, which is 15 bytes.

parts.question: Apply merge 256 alone. How many ids does the text become?

feedback.correct: 13: `on` stands in two places, each saving one id.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the places where `o` is followed by `n`.

byKey.one-place: `on` appears in both `bonds` and `bond`, so two ids are saved, not one.
byKey.bytes: That is the count before the merge.

explain.text: `o n` occurs in `bonds` and in `bond`; `fund` has `u n`, a different pair. Two replacements take 15 ids to 13.

parts.question: Now apply all five merges in order. How many tokens is the text?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply each merge in turn to the row the last one left.

byKey.no-un: You stopped before merge 260. `fund` holds `u n`, which joins.
byKey.stop-258: You stopped before merges 259 and 260. The space before `bond` joins it, and `u n` joins in `fund`.

explain.text: After 256 to 259 the row is `bond s space f u n d  bond`, 8 ids; then 260 joins `u n`. That leaves 7 tokens.

parts.question: Using the 7 tokens from part 2, how many bytes per token does this text get? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the bytes by the tokens.

byKey.inverted: Your figure is below 1, which would mean a token holds less than a byte. Swap the division.

explain.text: The text is 15 bytes in 7 tokens, so $15 / 7 \approx 2.1429$.

parts.question: A model scores 4.1 nats per token on this text. Using $15 / 7$ bytes per token from part 3, what is its loss in bits per byte? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Share the loss among the bytes of a token, then turn nats into bits.

byKey.no-ln2: Your figure is still in nats. Convert it to bits with $\ln 2$.
byKey.per-token: Your figure is a whole token's loss in bits; a token here spans $15 / 7$ bytes.

explain.text: Spread over $15 / 7$ bytes, 4.1 nats become $4.1 \times 7 / 15$ nats each. In bits that is about 2.7604, after a division by $\ln 2$.

items.prose: A client register exports names to a settlement system whose name field holds a fixed number of bytes. One client is `Lefèvre & Søn`, 13 characters long.

parts.question: How many bytes is the name in UTF-8?

feedback.correct: 15: `è` and `ø` take 2 bytes each, the other 11 characters 1 each.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Give each character its UTF-8 byte count.

byKey.chars: That counts characters. `è` and `ø` take 2 bytes each.
byKey.three-each: `è` and `ø` are below U+0800, so they take 2 bytes, not 3.

explain.text: `è` is U+00E8 and `ø` is U+00F8, both in the two-byte range. So $11 + 2 + 2 = 15$ bytes.

parts.question: Using the byte counts from part 1, the field holds 12 bytes. A cut that never splits a character keeps how many characters?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add characters while their bytes still fit in 12.

byKey.twelve: 12 characters would include `ø`, ending at byte 14.
byKey.ten: `S` ends exactly at byte 12, so it fits.

explain.text: The bytes run up to 12 at `S`, since `è` used 2. The next character, `ø`, needs bytes 13 and 14, so the cut keeps 11 characters.

parts.question: Unlike the safe cut of part 2, another system cuts the raw bytes at 13 and decodes with `errors='replace'`. How many characters does it show, counting the replacement character?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Byte 13 is the first half of `ø`; what does `replace` do with it?

byKey.ignore: That is what `errors='ignore'` would show. `replace` adds U+FFFD in place of the broken byte.
byKey.both-bytes: Only one byte of `ø` survived; the broken sequence becomes a single U+FFFD.

explain.text: The first 12 bytes decode to 11 characters, and the lone first byte of `ø` becomes one U+FFFD. That shows 12 characters.

parts.question: A byte-level tokeniser with no merges reads the whole name, the 15 bytes from part 1. How many tokens does it make?

feedback.generic: Not quite. With no merges, what is each token?

byKey.chars: Tokens are bytes here, not characters; `è` and `ø` are 2 tokens each.

explain.text: With no merges every byte is its own token. The name is 15 bytes, so 15 tokens.

items.prose: A research team builds a corpus of 12,400 earnings-call transcripts from several vendors, then scores a model on a held-out test set.

parts.question: Exact deduplication finds 9,850 distinct transcripts. How many does it remove?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the distinct transcripts from the total.

byKey.kept: That is the number kept, not removed.

explain.text: Each distinct transcript is kept once, so $12400 - 9850 = 2550$ are removed.

parts.question: Two remaining transcripts have 1,200 and 1,150 distinct shingles, 1,100 of them shared. What is their Jaccard similarity? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Jaccard puts the shared count over the count in either set.

byKey.over-first: You divided by one set's size. Use the union, $1200 + 1150 - 1100$.
byKey.over-sum: You divided by the sum of the sizes, which counts the shared ones twice.

parts.question: Using the similarity of 0.88 from part 2, does a filter with threshold 0.85 flag the pair?

options.why: The filter sees only the score; 0.88 clears the 0.85 threshold.

options.text: No: only identical texts are flagged
options.why: That is exact deduplication. A near-duplicate filter flags scores at least its threshold.

feedback.correct: The pair is flagged as near duplicates.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the score with the threshold.

explain.text: 0.88 is at least 0.85, so the filter flags the pair, and one of the two is dropped. A reader should check the pair does not differ in a key figure.

parts.question: The test set has 400 transcripts, and 36 of them also sit in the training corpus. What percentage of the test set leaked?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the leaked transcripts by the test set's size.

byKey.count: You typed the count of 36 as a percentage. Give the share of the 400.
byKey.over-train: You divided by the deduplicated corpus. The share asked is of the 400 test transcripts.
byKey.over-raw: You divided by the training corpus. The share asked is of the 400 test transcripts.

explain.text: $36 / 400 = 0.09$, so 9% of the test transcripts were seen in training. Their loss will look better than the model deserves.

parts.question: After the clean-up the test loss is 2.2 nats per token. The tokeniser packs 4.0 bytes into each token here. Convert the loss to bits per byte, to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Spread the loss over the bytes in a token, then change nats to bits.

byKey.no-ln2: 0.55 is still in nats. A bit is worth $\ln 2$ nats.
byKey.per-token: That figure is per token. Share it among the 4 bytes.

explain.text: Each byte carries $2.2 / 4 = 0.55$ nats, and 0.55 nats is $0.55 / \ln 2$ bits. That comes to about 0.7935.
